title: Counter programs on a single tape

based_on.title: Computation Theory
based_on.venue: University of Cambridge, Part IB lecture slides, based on Andrew Pitts's notes
based_on.pages: Slides 20–25, 27–32, 77 (register instructions, examples and the register-to-tape simulation sketch)

summary: Compile increment, consuming decrement and halt into a finite tape machine, preserving every register step and the exact native output.
abstract: A program can add two numbers by repeatedly subtracting one from one register and adding one to another. Each register holds a natural number, but a tape machine can read and change only one finite symbol at a time. Writing the registers as parallel rows of unary bits turns increment and decrement into scans that return to a marked origin. A finite transition table implements these scans and preserves the other registers. When the counter program halts, a final sweep moves the chosen output onto the machine's distinguished mark track and erases the origin and every auxiliary track. The resulting native tape machine has exactly the same halting inputs and numerical outputs as the counter program, and a counter computation that never halts yields a tape computation that never halts. The construction works for any fixed finite number of registers and finite program, with explicit input and output conventions.
